title: The FLUXNET2015 dataset and the ONEFlux processing pipeline for eddy covariance data
problem: Non-uniform processing and quality control across independently-managed global eddy covariance sites create data heterogeneity, which limits intercomparability and hampers robust, global-scale synthesis studies and uncertainty quantification.
method: This paper presents the ONEFlux open-source processing pipeline, which applies uniform methods for quality control, gap-filling, flux partitioning, and uncertainty estimation to produce the globally consistent and intercomparable FLUXNET2015 eddy covariance dataset from data voluntarily contributed by hundreds of sites.
task: This paper describes the FLUXNET2015 dataset, providing globally standardized ecosystem-scale CO2, water, and energy exchange data, and details the open-source ONEFlux processing pipeline used to generate it from eddy covariance measurements.
innovation: This paper details the FLUXNET2015 dataset, providing ecosystem-scale data on CO₂, water, and energy exchange from 212 global sites, and describes the open-source ONEFlux processing pipeline used for its creation, which includes uniform methods for quality control, gap-filling, and uncertainty quantification.

The FLUXNET2015 dataset and the ONEFlux processing pipeline for eddy covariance data

FLUXNET was created as a global network of networks16–18, a joint effort among regional networks to harmonize and increase standardization of the data being collected. It made possible the creation of global eddy covariance datasets. The first gap-filled, global FLUXNET dataset, which included derived, partitioned fluxes like photosynthesis and respiration, was the Marconi dataset¹⁰ in 2000, with 97 site-years of data, followed by the 2007 La Thuile dataset20 with 965 site-years of data, and finally in 2015 the FLUXNET2015 dataset18,21 (hereafter FLUXNET2015) with 1532 site-years of data.

For over three decades, the eddy covariance technique¹ has been used to measure land-atmosphere exchanges of greenhouse gases and energy at sites around the world to study and determine the function and trajectories of both ecosystems and the climate system.

The FLUXNET2015 dataset provides ecosystem-scale data on CO2, water, and energy exchange between the biosphere and the atmosphere, and other meteorological and biological measurements, from 212 sites around the globe (over 1500 site-years, up to and including year 2014).

CP and MP USTAR threshold methods. Two methods to calculate USTAR thresholds were used: change-point-detection (CP) proposed by Barr et al.41 and a modified version of the moving-point-transition (MP) described originally by Reichstein et al.31 and Papale et al.30.

CO2 products. The processing steps applied to CO2 fluxes were: calculation of net ecosystem exchange (NEE) from CO2 turbulent and storage fluxes, applying a spike detection algorithm, filtering for low turbulence conditions using multiple friction velocity (USTAR) thresholds, gap-filling of all NEE time series generated by an ensemble of USTAR thresholds, estimation of random uncertainty, and partitioning of NEE into its ecosystem respiration (RECO) and gross primary production (GPP) components.

The processing steps applied to CO2 fluxes were: calculation of net ecosystem exchange (NEE) from CO2 turbulent and storage fluxes, applying a spike detection algorithm, filtering for low turbulence conditions using multiple friction velocity (USTAR) thresholds, gap-filling of all NEE time series generated by an ensemble of USTAR thresholds, estimation of random uncertainty, and partitioning of NEE into its ecosystem respiration (RECO) and gross primary production (GPP) components.

Partitioning CO2 fluxes from NEE into estimates of its two main components, Gross Primary Production (GPP) and Ecosystem Respiration (RECO), was done by parameterizations of models using measured data. All sites were partitioned with the nighttime fluxes method³¹ (_NT suffixes) and the daytime fluxes method43 (_DT suffixes), while a third method, sundown reference respiration44 (_SR suffixes), was applied to all sites meeting the method's requirements (e.g., high quality storage measurement).

Steps implemented in python. The main controller code for ONEFlux is implemented in Python. Besides being the glue code that executes each step, pre- and post-checks are also executed before and after each step. These checks guarantee that the input data meet the minimum requirements to run the step, that the minimum expected outputs were generated by the execution of the step, and that any errors or exception conditions were handled correctly.
Steps implemented in C. Several steps are implemented in the C programming language, allowing better control over execution performance of these steps.

Steps implemented in MATLAB. The estimation of USTAR thresholds using the CP method (05_ustar_cp) is the only step implemented in MATLAB. It is distributed both as source code and compiled code to be used with the MATLAB Runtime Environment, such that it does not require a license purchase.
